title: America's Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent portrays the U.S. as an angry god, demanding allies submit as if to Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through the editorial: the louder the threat, the more it proves the U.S. lacks the means to follow through, and allies are already hedging.
why: Offers a contrarian reading of a seemingly tough Treasury editorial: theological threats rarely materialize, and understanding this helps predict allies' true leverage in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers in cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risks, and policy researchers trying to gauge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription pitch; start directly with Carney's speech and Bessent's editorial.

points.h: The Treasury chief casts the U.S. as an angry god
points.body: In Bessent's Financial Times editorial on "economic D-Day," he frames allies' choice as a Pascal's wager. Farrell's read: he's essentially saying you must treat the U.S. as God and appease this wrathful deity by any means, or it will strike you with lightning. Farrell likens it to a 17th-century Puritan sermon, which could be titled "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," except the sinners are the rest of the world. The problem: such sermonizing threats are usually a reaction when the pastor senses the congregation drifting away, not a sign of strength.

points.h: The louder the shout, the softer the stick
points.body: Roosevelt's maxim was "speak softly and carry a big stick." Farrell says Bessent's approach is the reverse: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China: it is currently the country most capable of supporting Iran, and Bessent doesn't want to answer whether the U.S. would dare to bring its wrath down on China if it continues buying Iranian oil. Farrell believes markets and nations are betting "it won't." So the editorial reads more like an empty threat—the more it overpromises, the more it shows the U.S. bluffing at an empty table.

points.h: Flexible realism equals no strategy at all
points.body: Using "flexible realism" to explain White House behavior is just covering chaos with a cloth. Farrell says the term, unpacked, means only one thing: the U.S. does whatever it wants, and other countries should adapt. What actually drives the White House is not strategy but a scramble for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone revolve around him—but Trump does "a stupid version" of that: as long as he can be the center of everyone's attention, he'll make decisions that are extremely foolish in both the long and short term. Other countries' response, therefore, becomes damage control rather than continued betting.

Federalist Paper No. 10 offered the answer: "ambition must be made to counteract ambition," letting each person's drive for power cancel out the others, grinding toward an equilibrium close to the public interest. Farrell says this mechanism has been dismantled from both ends. One end is the Republican Party: internal dissent has nearly vanished; senators won't openly block even if they object; same-party control of all three branches short-circuits the original checks. The other end is the federal bureaucracy: the Supreme Court embraces the "unitary executive" theory, inspectors general are fired or intimidated, and ordinary civil servants are converted to at-will employees. With a fundamentally incompetent person at the top, errors are amplified into national madness.

points.h: Rebuilding U.S. institutions requires learning to experiment
points.body: Farrell doesn't think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he also doesn't think the U.S. is doomed to slide into disaster. The model he points to is New York Mayor Mamdani's experiment: building feedback loops between city government and the public, turning people's real troubles into policy, and using social media to show the public "I'm listening and acting." He explicitly links this style to Roosevelt's "bold, persistent experimentation": keep what works, discard what doesn't. The open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying "this path didn't work, let's try another"—without that tolerance, experiments won't go far.

points.h: The more flexible, the less anyone takes you seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that is depleted by capriciousness: credibility. Farrell cites Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling's argument that one of a nation's most important assets is credibility; promises and threats that can be carried out are what actually work in negotiations. If you change your mind at will, and threats made with conviction one day vanish the next, eventually no one takes you seriously. Farrell believes the U.S. is in that state today: other nations still fear its capacity to cause harm but no longer believe in its ability to act consistently over time. His image: a drunk grandfather holding a shotgun—everyone just humors him to keep him from firing.

points.h: America is smashing its own web with a sledgehammer
points.body: The core argument in Farrell and Newman's "Underground Empire" is that globalization is a web of interdependence—supply chains are stitched together by thousands of suppliers across dozens of countries, and dollar clearing is the nervous system of that web. The U.S. built this system with one hand while reserving a "house advantage" with the other, using the threat of cutting off access to discipline others. The Trump administration's approach is not to delicately dismantle the web but to swing a sledgehammer semi-randomly at various parts. Farrell's direction is clear: full decoupling would be a disaster; what nations can do is not to go independent but to make interdependence resilient, while major powers relearn the language of "restraint."

points.h: A rare-earth card punctures the myth of inevitable victory
points.body: On last year's "Liberation Day," Bessent publicly said the U.S. held all the aces and China had no cards. Weeks later, China played its rare-earth and critical-minerals card, and the U.S. suddenly realized it was holding a busted flush—a hand that looked strong but never materialized. Farrell sees this as the moment that sobered the U.S. side; since then, speeches by Marco Rubio and others reflect that recognition: China has the capacity to materially harm the U.S. economy. The U.S. and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows "I can hurt you badly," but they have not yet sat down to turn that balance into more stable rules.
